stages.title: TERMINOLOGY FIREWALL: INDUSTRY, MANUFACTURING, FACTORY AND INDUSTRIAL REGION
stages.terms: Trap: Manufacturing data, factory-sector data and employment generated by a scheme have different boundaries.
stages.mechanism: Trap: Manufacturing data, factory-sector data and employment generated by a scheme have different boundaries.
stages.consequence: A factory is an establishment or production site; it is not automatically the whole industry.
stages.trap: Manufacturing data, factory-sector data and employment generated by a scheme have different boundaries.
stages.answer: Mini recap: Industry is the ecosystem; manufacturing is the activity; factory is the site; region is the connected landscape.

stages.title: MAIN LOCATION FACTORS: BUILD A RANKED FACTOR SYSTEM
stages.terms: Visual first: location results from interacting material, energy, labour, market, transport, water, capital and technology pulls.
stages.mechanism: Visual first: location results from interacting material, energy, labour, market, transport, water, capital and technology pulls.
stages.consequence: Rank the factors; do not merely list them.
stages.trap: No single factor explains all industries, and one industry can have different orientations at different stages.
stages.answer: Sugar mills are pulled toward cane because cane is bulky and loses recoverable quality with delay.

stages.title: WEBER'S LEAST-COST THEORY: LEARN IT IN SIX STEPS
stages.terms: Alfred Weber's 1909 model asks: where can a factory minimise the combined burden of transport cost, labour cost and agglomeration/deglomeration effects?
stages.mechanism: A firm moves to a labour site only when labour savings exceed that extra freight burden.
stages.consequence: It is the starting point, not an automatic final answer.
stages.trap: Weber did not explain transport alone; labour and agglomeration are central to the model.
stages.answer: The first task is to find the site with the lowest total cost of moving inputs in and output out.

stages.title: TYPES OF INDUSTRIAL ORIENTATION: COMPARE STAGES, NOT LABELS
stages.terms: Visual first: a value chain can contain source-oriented, power-oriented, market-oriented and knowledge-oriented stages.
stages.mechanism: Technology can split the chain: raw-material processing remains near the source while assembly or finishing moves toward markets.
stages.consequence: Steel's mining and beneficiation remain source-linked, while some finishing operations can move closer to automobile and construction markets.
stages.trap: Footloose means flexible among suitable sites, not free from skills, utilities, logistics or regulation.
stages.answer: The term “orientation” does not imprison an industry in one place.

stages.title: MAJOR WORLD INDUSTRIAL REGIONS: MAP THE MECHANISM BEHIND EACH BELT
stages.terms: Use world cases to prove mechanisms, not as decorative examples: Japan refutes resource determinism; Ruhr/Great Lakes show conditional inertia; coastal China shows policy-enabled export agglomeration.
stages.mechanism: Use world cases to prove mechanisms, not as decorative examples: Japan refutes resource determinism; Ruhr/Great Lakes show conditional inertia; coastal China shows policy-enabled export agglomeration.
stages.consequence: Use these as textbook locational frames, not undated rank claims.
stages.trap: Contemporary output leadership can shift. Use these as textbook locational frames, not undated rank claims.
stages.answer: Visual first: the world's major regions represent different combinations of resources, ports, markets, labour and state-supported infrastructure; the map is schematic and not to scale.

stages.title: AGGLOMERATION, DEGLOMERATION AND INDUSTRIAL INERTIA
stages.terms: Agglomeration means firms cluster because they share.
stages.mechanism: Industrial inertia means an old industrial centre continues after its original reason weakens because sunk infrastructure, skills, institutions, suppliers and market relationships remain valuable.
stages.consequence: Trap: Inertia is not a guarantee of survival; it is a mechanism that can be overcome by technological, market or ecological change.
stages.trap: Inertia is not a guarantee of survival; it is a mechanism that can be overcome by technological, market or ecological change.
stages.answer: Yet inertia is not permanent if technology, demand and transferable skills erode.

stages.title: ACTORS, INSTITUTIONS AND PLANNED LOCATION: THE STATE CAN SUPPORT, NOT INVENT, EVERY LINKAGE
stages.terms: Trap: An industrial corridor is not simply a highway; it is an integrated manufacturing-freight-urban-utility system.
stages.mechanism: The location-theory link is valid: transport, land, labour pools, utilities and market reach are being assembled through policy.
stages.consequence: A corridor can lower entry cost for firms, but it becomes an industrial region only when suppliers, workers, housing, services and repeated production linkages accumulate.
stages.trap: An industrial corridor is not simply a highway; it is an integrated manufacturing-freight-urban-utility system.
stages.answer: Mini recap: The state can coordinate location and manufacture initial agglomeration, but firms and local linkages must make it self-sustaining.

stages.title: WHAT CHANGED AFTER WEBER - AND WHAT DID NOT
stages.terms: A balanced assessment says classical theory is a starting lens, not a universal law.
stages.mechanism: A semiconductor or electronics location depends on reliable power, water, specialised suppliers, skills, air-sea connectivity and customer qualification.
stages.consequence: A balanced assessment says classical theory is a starting lens, not a universal law.
stages.trap: Digitalisation reduces some distance costs but does not erase the geography of people, energy, logistics or regulation.
stages.answer: It is not “location-free”; its cost surface is simply more complex than a mine-market triangle.
